cards.text: Here's a psalm of David, written for the choirmaster. It opens by calling somebody blessed. And when a psalm does that, friend, you lean IN, because somebody's about to get some GOOD news.

cards.question: At the start of Psalm 41, who does David call blessed?

answers.text: The one who cares for the poor
The one who gives at the temple
The one who keeps every feast

cards.text: Caring for the poor doesn't go unnoticed. David says that even on that person's worst day, the day of trouble, the LORD gets involved.

cards.question: David says the LORD will ___ the one who cares for the poor in the day of trouble.

cards.text: Then David keeps STACKING it: the LORD will protect him, preserve him and bless him in the land. That's not one blessing, friend, that's a whole cookie BOX!

cards.question: True or false: David says the LORD will give the one who cares for the poor over to the will of his foes.

cards.text: Now picture that same person sick, stuck in bed. Let's see where the LORD is in that moment.

cards.question: When the one who cares for the poor is lying sick in bed, what does the LORD do for him?

cards.text: Then the psalm turns. David stops describing someone else and starts praying for HIMSELF.

cards.question: When David starts praying for himself, what does he ask the LORD to do?
True or false: David asks the LORD for grace while telling Him he has done nothing wrong.

cards.text: No excuses, no fine print. David just says it: "I have sinned against You." Meanwhile I burn ONE batch and I'm blaming the oven, the timer AND the weather.
Then David tells what his enemies are saying about him. And I promise you, friend, it is NOT a get-well card.

cards.question: What do David's enemies say about him with malice?

answers.text: When will he die and be forgotten
When will he leave this land for good
Who will take his place on the throne

cards.text: Then somebody comes to visit David, and a visit should be sweet: pull up a chair, bring a cookie. Let's see how this one goes.

cards.question: What does David's visitor do once he goes back out?

answers.text: Tells the priests he is well

cards.text: He came in SMILING and walked out with a whole REPORT. And now all who hate David are whispering against him.

cards.question: True or false: The people whispering against David say a vile disease has been poured into him and he will never get up from where he lies.

cards.text: Then David says the line that stings the most. Get ready, friend.

cards.question: Who does David say has lifted up his heel against him?
David's trusted friend shared his bread, so the two of them sat at the same ___.

cards.text: Lifted up his heel. That's not a nudge, that's a KICK, from somebody who ate at David's table. Centuries later, Jesus quotes this very line about Himself (John 13:18).
But David doesn't stay down there. He turns right back to God: "But You, O LORD…"

cards.question: With enemies whispering and a friend turned against him, what does David ask the LORD to do?

answers.text: Be gracious and raise him up
Send him far away from them
Let him hide until it passes

cards.text: David even says why he wants back up: so he can repay them. Flat on his back and already planning the comeback, while the big plan in MY drawer was counting dust.

cards.question: True or false: David says he knows the LORD delights in him because his enemy does not triumph over him.

cards.text: David says it's the LORD who upholds him in his integrity. Same as my gold base, friend: I don't hold it up, it holds ME up.

cards.question: David says the LORD sets him in His ___ forever.

cards.text: Then David wraps up the whole psalm. Watch how it lands, because it echoes the way it started.

cards.question: Psalm 41 opens by blessing the one who cares for the poor. It closes by blessing the ___.
How does David sign off at the very end of Psalm 41?

cards.text: From whispers and a kick from a friend all the way to "Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, from everlasting to everlasting." And not one Amen, friend, TWO, because some praise you just gotta sign twice.

findings.problem: "Even on that person's worst day" stretches "the day of trouble" (Ps 41:1). The text speaks of a day of trouble. It does not call it his worst day.

rule.text: Don't stretch the text. Exaggerate only in his own jokes.

findings.problem: Cards 3 to 6 already show the LORD delivering, protecting, preserving and blessing this person. That makes "Leaves him to rest alone" and "Hides His face from him" easy to rule out. Only the right answer is believable, so the card is a giveaway rather than an informed guess.

rule.text: Wrong answers for what someone does or says only need to be believable.

findings.problem: "David stops describing someone else" says the one who cares for the poor (Ps 41:1-3) is a different person from David. The text leaves open how the blessed one in verses 1-3 connects to the speaker in verse 4.

rule.text: Leave open what the text leaves open: who is being spoken to, why, or how two things connect.

findings.problem: This story card only restates verse 4, which card 11 already covered (David admits sin rather than claiming innocence). It does not move the baker forward through the passage.
The question says the whisperers "say" the vile disease line. In the text, the quote is introduced by "they imagine the worst for me" (Ps 41:7-8), not by a verb of saying.

rule.text: Call things what the text calls them.

findings.problem: The question tests an inference the text never states. Verse 9 says the friend "shared my bread." It says nothing about sitting at a table. The question already gives away the actual detail (shared bread) and asks only for an inferred word. It adds nothing the baker needs to understand the passage.

rule.text: Ask about the moments that move the passage forward and the details the baker needs to understand it.

findings.problem: No earlier card sets up "presence" (Ps 41:12). Card 15 covers only being upheld in integrity. Choosing between presence, palace and army is a guess at wording the baker hasn't seen, not meaning they can reason out.

rule.text: The blank tests meaning the baker can reason out, not wording they haven't seen.

findings.problem: Asking how David signs off (Amen and Amen, Selah and Selah, or Hallelujah and Hallelujah) asks the baker to guess the exact closing words of the line, not its movement or meaning.

rule.text: Never ask the baker to guess the next words of a line.

findings.problem: Cards 17, 19 and 20 present Psalm 41:13 as David's own sign-off ("Then David wraps up the whole psalm", "How does David sign off"). Verse 13 is widely read as the doxology that closes Book I of the Psalms, not part of David's psalm. The superscription credits the psalm to David, and the passage includes verse 13.
findings.question: Should Papa Dorin attribute the closing doxology of a psalm book (like Ps 41:13, 72:18-19, 89:52, 106:48) to the psalm's named author? Or should he present it neutrally, without saying who added it?
